title: Rethinking Multi-Branch and Cross-Backbone Fusion for Vehicle Re-Identification in the Foundation-Model Era
abstract: Multi-branch architectures and CNN-Transformer fusion have long been regarded as effective ways to improve vehicle re-identification (Re-ID) by combining complementary representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption in the foundation-model era through a comprehensive empirical study. A single DINOv3-pretrained ConvNeXt trained with a tuned recipe achieves 88.19 mAP on VeRi-Wild Small and 77.47 mAP on VeRi-Wild Large using visual cues alone, matching the strongest protocol-verified metadata-dependent multi-branch baseline. Applying training-free re-ranking further improves performance to 92.38 and 83.68 mAP, respectively. Using this strong baseline together with retrieval-level branch diagnostics, we evaluate whether increasing representational diversity still provides measurable gains. Across both benchmarks, concatenating multiple branches built on a shared backbone changes the best single-branch performance by less than one mAP point while increasing the embedding dimension by 4x, and the resulting representation has an effective rank close to the original feature dimension. We further study cross-backbone fusion using an asymmetric frozen-anchor strategy to combine ConvNeXt and Vision Transformer representations. Despite these favorable conditions, Transformer branches consistently remain 13-15 mAP below the ConvNeXt backbone, and paired per-query bootstrap analysis estimates the largest observed fusion gain to be only +0.11 mAP (95% confidence interval). Our results suggest that, under the evaluated setting, improving a single strong foundation-model backbone together with retrieval-stage re-ranking is more effective than increasing architectural complexity through additional branches or heterogeneous backbones. We restrict our conclusions to single-seed training and one family of foundation models and discuss conditions under which these observations may not hold.

Rethinking Multi-Branch and Cross-Backbone Fusion for Vehicle Re-Identification in the Foundation-Model Era Yu Wang 1 {}^{\textbf{1}} and Hongyu Yang 1 {}^{\textbf{1}} Huahuan (Yunnan) Technology Co., Ltd., Yunnan, China Abstract Multi-branch architectures and CNN–Transformer fusion are widely believed to improve vehicle re-identification (Re-ID) by combining complementary representations. We revisit this assumption in the foundation-model era. A single DINOv3-pretrained ConvNeXt with a tuned recipe reaches 88.19 mAP on VeRi-Wild Small and 77.47 on Large from visual cues alone , matching the strongest protocol-verified metadata-dependent multi-branch baseline, and 92.38/83.68 with training-free re-ranking . Armed with this baseline and retrieval-level branch diagnostics, we ask whether representational diversity still pays at this scale. It does not. Across both benchmarks and every configuration we train, concatenating multiple heads over a shared backbone moves the best single head by under one mAP point in either direction while costing four times the embedding dimension, and the concatenation has an effective rank near 512. Pushing diversity to its architectural limit, CNN versus Transformer, we grant fusion every advantage through an asymmetric frozen-anchor scheme . Every Transformer configuration still lands 13–15 mAP below the ConvNeXt backbone, and a paired per-query bootstrap bounds the fusion gain at + 0.11 +0.11 mAP (95% CI) even for the most favourable fusion snapshot we obtained. One strong backbone with the right recipe and re-ranking is the efficiency frontier. All results use single-seed training and one foundation-model family; we scope claims accordingly and list falsifiers. {IEEEkeywords} Cross-camera evaluation, feature fusion, foundation models, multi-branch networks, re-ranking, representation similarity, vehicle re-identification, vision transformers. 1 Introduction \IEEEPARstart Vehicle re-identification (Re-ID)—matching a query vehicle across non-overlapping cameras—is a core capability for intelligent transportation systems, underpinning cross-camera tracking, traffic analytics, and urban surveillance [ 3 , 1 ] . For nearly a decade, progress in vehicle and person Re-ID has been driven by representational diversity . Multi-branch and multi-granularity networks split features into parallel streams [ 4 , 5 ] ; part-based and jigsaw modules extract local descriptors [ 6 ] ; and a growing line of work fuses heterogeneous backbones—typically a CNN with a Transformer—on the premise that their complementary inductive biases yield retrieval cues that neither captures alone [ 7 ] . The shared, rarely questioned assumption is that more diverse representations are better : each branch contributes unique correct matches, and their aggregation surpasses any single stream [ 5 , 4 ] . That assumption was established with ImageNet-pretrained, lightweight backbones, where no single extractor was near saturation and diversity was a cheap path to coverage. Foundation models change the premise. DINOv3 already rivals specialized state of the art without fine-tuning [ 8 ] , and in Re-ID simply fine-tuning a foundation encoder is competitive with elaborate architectures [ 9 ] —such a backbone may capture most of the signal a task affords, leaving little headroom for extra branches. Fine-tuning is also known to distort pretrained features [ 10 ] , casting doubt on whether branch diversity, even if present at initialization, survives joint optimization. Whether the premise holds at this scale has, to our knowledge, never been tested—yet it governs how practitioners spend compute: on one strong backbone, or on several fused ones. We re-examine it on VeRi-Wild [ 1 ] and VeRi-776 [ 2 ] under the official cross-camera protocol, whose omission we show inflates reported numbers by 3–4 mAP. We first establish that a single DINOv3-ConvNeXt [ 8 , 11 ] , given a tuned recipe (pure-ConvNeXt heads, full unfreezing, full data, staged LR decay), reaches parity with the strongest metadata-dependent published multi-branch baseline—echoing, at foundation-model scale, that training procedure can matter as much as architecture [ 12 , 13 ] . Against this baseline we stress-test diversity with a reusable diagnostic toolkit. Crucially, we do not stop at a naïve fusion that could be dismissed as under-engineered. We diagnose why symmetric joint fine-tuning of two foundation backbones collapses—a learning rate tolerable for one erodes both, and the fusion’s apparent + 4.9 +4.9 gain is measured against a jointly degraded base—then give fusion every advantage: an asymmetric frozen-anchor scheme that freezes the strong 88.19 ConvNeXt as a semantic anchor and trains only the Transformer and the fusion module, under three independent recipes plus a LoRA control , ruling out the objection that the weaker branch was merely under-trained. Our findings are consistently negative for the diversity premise—and, we argue, this is the contribution. Multiple heads over a shared backbone become more alike with training, not less—consistent with the view that solutions sharing an optimization trajectory occupy a single mode in function space, whereas ensemble diversity classically derives from independent training [ 14 , 15 ] . Cross-backbone heterogeneity, by contrast, is genuine and survives training (top-10 Jaccard 0.54 against 0.79–0.84 for same-backbone heads), in line with documented representational differences between ViTs and CNNs [ 16 ] —yet it is not fusible: the Transformer branch never crosses a ∼ 73 {\sim}73 mAP ceiling under any recipe, and an oracle fusion of our strongest Transformer with the single backbone assigns it weight zero. Diversity is not sufficient; it must be aggregable, and here it is not. We contribute: • (i) the first systematic evidence that the diversity premise fails under foundation-model-scale fine-tuning, in two distinct ways: same-backbone multi-branch heads collapse into redundancy (replicated in-domain on both VeRi-Wild and VeRi-776), while cross-backbone CNN–Transformer diversity survives yet proves unfusible —an oracle score-level fusion of our strongest ViT assigns it weight zero (established under VeRi-Wild training); • (ii) a documented training recipe that lifts a single DINOv3-ConvNeXt to parity with the strongest protocol-verified metadata-dependent published multi-branch baseline (MBR-4B-LAI, the camera/view-conditioned variant of MBR) on VeRi-Wild; • (iii) a branch-level diagnostic toolkit—complementing representation-level similarity analyses [ 17 , 18 ] with retrieval-level measures—and a convergence-only measurement discipline that we show is essential, as undertrained snapshots systematically mislead; • (iv) a deployment-oriented efficiency frontier: a single backbone plus a memory-scalable, mathematically exact sparse re-ranking [ 19 ] matches metadata-dependent baselines [ 5 , 6 ] at roughly one-third the inference cost of dual-backbone fusion ( 2.8 × 2.8\times lower latency, 3 × 3\times fewer FLOPs). 2 Related Work Vehicle Re-ID. The field has matured from metric learning on VehicleID [ 20 ] to in-the-wild benchmarks such as VeRi-776 [ 2 ] and VeRi-Wild [ 1 ] , with recent methods exploiting multi-branch topologies, viewpoint/attribute metadata and Transformer backbones [ 3 ] . Two properties of the vehicle setting—strong inter-class similarity between same-model vehicles, and severe viewpoint variation—have made representational diversity an attractive design principle: precisely the premise we revisit. Multi-branch and multi-granularity Re-ID. Splitting features into parallel streams is a dominant design: MGN [ 4 ] combines a global branch with partitioned local branches; MBR [ 5 ] pairs a ResNet50-IBN global branch with a BoT self-attention branch under a Loss-Branch-Split strategy, explicitly attributing its gains to “improved feature diversity”; TransReID [ 6 ] adds jigsaw patch rearrangement to a pure-Transformer baseline; FusionReID [ 7 ] fuses CNN and Transformer features through stacked mutual-attention modules, premised on complementary inductive biases. Bag-of-Tricks [ 13 ] is an early counterpoint, showing a single global stream with careful training rivals multi-branch designs. Across this line, diversity is asserted and validated only through end-to-end mAP ablations; no work measures whether branches actually retrieve differently . We supply exactly that measurement—and find that, at foundation-model scale, they do not. Foundation models and fine-tuning. DINOv3 [ 8 ] shows a single self-supervised backbone can match specialized state of the art without fine-tuning; CLIP-ReID [ 9 ] shows that merely fine-tuning a foundation image encoder is already competitive in Re-ID, and CLIP-based semantic enhancement reports among the highest published VeRi-Wild figures [ 21 ] (89.1 mAP, without a public implementation and without a stated test split)—not established to be protocol-comparable to our filtered numbers, a gap smaller than the protocol inflation we measure (Section 4-4.2 , Table 2 ). Kumar et al. [ 10 ] prove that full fine-tuning distorts pretrained features and can underperform out-of-distribution, motivating freezing strategies; layer-wise LR decay [ 22 ] is the standard mitigation. What joint fine-tuning does to multi-branch topologies built atop such backbones has not been examined; we show it homogenizes them. Representation similarity and ensemble diversity. CKA [ 17 ] and its applications [ 18 , 16 ] characterize when networks learn similar representations—notably, that ViTs and CNNs differ substantially [ 16 ] , and that models with equal accuracy can still err differently [ 18 ] . Deep ensembles [ 15 ] derive their gains from independently trained members; Fort et al. [ 14 ] show that solutions along a shared optimization trajectory cluster in a single function-space mode, while independent initializations explore distinct modes. Our diagnostics extend this literature from representation- and classification-level to retrieval-level measures, and our findings instantiate the shared-trajectory prediction in the multi-branch Re-ID setting. 3 Evaluation Protocol and Preliminaries Datasets and splits. VeRi-Wild [ 1 ] : we report the official test_3000 split (3,000 query IDs, 38,861 gallery images; “Small”) and test_10000 (128,517 gallery; “Large”). VeRi-776 [ 2 ] serves as a cross-domain target: models trained on VeRi-Wild are evaluated on VeRi-776 without seeing it. Protocol discipline. All numbers use the official cross-camera evaluation: gallery images sharing both the query’s vehicle ID and camera are excluded as junk, along with the query itself. Table 1 quantifies why this matters on our own reproductions: omitting the filter inflates mAP by + 3.04 +3.04 on VeRi-776 and + 3.94 +3.94 on VeRi-Wild . We verified our protocol reproduces the original MBR evaluation code’s behavior exactly. All comparisons in this paper are protocol-matched; we flag this as a reproduction pitfall—inflated, unfiltered numbers land close enough to filtered published figures to cause silent misranking—rather than as a claim that any specific published pipeline omitted the filter. For unit-normalized per-branch embeddings f 1 , … , f B f_{1},\dots,f_{B} , stacking them and re-normalizing by B \sqrt{B} gives F = 1 B ​ [ f 1 ; … ; f B ] F=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{B}}[f_{1};\dots;f_{B}] , so the cosine similarity between two images a , b a,b is ⟨ F a , F b ⟩ = 1 B ​ ∑ i = 1 B ⟨ f i , a , f i , b ⟩ \langle F_{a},F_{b}\rangle=\tfrac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\langle f_{i,a},f_{i,b}\rangle —the arithmetic mean of the per-branch cosines. Proposition 1. Concatenation can outperform its best branch only if branches disagree in their retrieval orderings. Proof. If all branches induce the same ranking of the gallery for every query, then the mean similarity is a monotone (order-preserving) combination of identical orderings and therefore reproduces that common ranking; retrieval metrics (mAP, CMC) depend only on the ranking, so the concatenation equals every branch and cannot exceed the best. Hence a strict gain requires at least one query on which two branches order the gallery differently. □ \square This elementary fact underpins all diagnostics in Section 5 : measuring inter-branch disagreement (Jaccard, complementary-correctness) directly measures the headroom available to concatenation. 4 A Single Foundation Backbone Is (Almost) All You Need 4.1 Architecture and recipe Our model (“Option A”) is deliberately not novel: a single DINOv3-distilled ConvNeXt-Base backbone [ 8 , 11 ] under MBR’s Loss-Branch-Split topology [ 5 ] —four heads (two convolutional heads conv-cls, conv-metric, and two Bottleneck-Transformer (BoT) heads BoT-cls, BoT-metric [ 13 ] ), each producing a 2048-d embedding, concatenated to 8192-d—trained with cross-entropy and metric losses (Circle [ 23 ] , Center [ 24 ] , and Triplet [ 25 ] ). What is tuned is the recipe : (a) full-depth features; (b) full backbone unfreezing after a frozen warm-up phase; (c) full training data; (d) staged LR decay ( × 0.1 \times 0.1 at epoch 40). Training runs on 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs (a cloud server) with P 16 16 K 4 4 sampling—16 identities per GPU, 4 images each, i.e. an effective batch of 16 × 4 × 8 = 512 16\times 4\times 8=512 . Each recipe component maps to a step-like jump: frozen Phase 1 ends at 39.46 mAP; unfreezing jumps to 56.25 in one epoch ( + 16.8 +16.8 ); a steady climb to 85.98 by epoch 31; the epoch-40 LR decay adds + 2.21 +2.21 , converging at 88.19 (epoch 42). A component ablation (Section 5-5.2 ) attributes most of this gain to the LR-decay stage and shows the full-depth choice is dataset-dependent (it reverses on VeRi-776). 4.2 Results: metadata-free matches metadata-dependent Table 2 reports our main VeRi-Wild results, protocol-matched to [ 5 ] . Our margins over the strongest metadata-dependent variant MBR-4B-LAI are 0.07 (Small) and 0.06 (Large); against the metadata-free MBR-4B they widen to 0.22/0.32. All are far smaller than the evaluation’s own uncertainty: a query-level bootstrap (2,000 resamples) yields a 95% confidence interval of ± 0.66 \pm 0.66 mAP on Small (88.19, CI [87.51, 88.83]) and ± 0.51 \pm 0.51 on Large (77.47, CI [76.94, 77.95]) —wider than the LAI margin by nearly an order of magnitude ( ± 0.66 \pm 0.66 vs. 0.07, ≈ 9 × {\approx}9\times ). We therefore claim parity, not superiority , and we scope the parity claim to the protocol-verified comparison: purely visual features now match the strongest metadata-dependent configuration of the strongest published multi-branch baseline, removing camera/view annotations from the requirements list. CMC-1 reaches 96.39 (Small) / 91.86 (Large). The bootstrap CI quantifies evaluation uncertainty only; as these are single-seed runs (Section 7 ), the parity holds for our runs and we do not claim statistical superiority. We claim parity only with the strongest protocol-verified baseline and do not claim to lead the published leaderboard. 4.3 Cross-domain generalization Evaluated zero-shot on VeRi-776 (never seen in training), Option A reaches 66.02 mAP / 87.07 R1 (+re-ranking: 69.27). As a matched in-domain reference we use the same Option A architecture trained in-domain on VeRi-776 (84.07 mAP, Section 5-5.2 ); this remains below self-reported specialized systems we could not protocol-verify (e.g. CLIP-SENet 92.9 on VeRi-776 [ 21 ] ). Relative to this matched in-domain reference, the − 18.0 -18.0 mAP gap with an intact R1 of 87.07 indicates the model learned generic vehicle discrimination rather than overfitting the source domain; the degradation is consistent with fine-tuning’s known out-of-distribution cost [ 10 ] and with domain differences in camera count and day/night composition. 4.4 Exact sparse re-ranking at scale k k -reciprocal re-ranking [ 19 ] is the deployment workhorse ( + 4.19 +4.19 Small / + 6.21 +6.21 Large, with R1 preserved), but its classical implementation is memory-bound: on test_10000 it requires ∼ 190 {\sim}190 GB and fails outright. Our sparse implementation is mathematically exact —identical output to the classical algorithm on test_3000 ( Δ \Delta mAP = 0.0000 =0.0000 )—while running 18 × 18\times faster (29 s vs. 534 s) and completing test_10000 in 137 s within tens of GB. All timings are wall-clock on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090. Larger galleries benefit more from re-ranking, so removing the memory wall matters precisely where the gain is largest. We use the standard k k -reciprocal hyper-parameters k 1 = 20 k_{1}=20 , k 2 = 6 k_{2}=6 , λ = 0.3 \lambda=0.3 [ 19 ] ; the sparse form is mathematically exact—the identity ∑ p max ⁡ ( v i ​ p , v j ​ p ) = s i + s j − M i ​ j \sum_{p}\max(v_{ip},v_{jp})=s_{i}+s_{j}-M_{ij} (row sums s i s_{i} , sparse overlaps M i ​ j = ∑ p min ⁡ ( v i ​ p , v j ​ p ) M_{ij}=\sum_{p}\min(v_{ip},v_{jp}) ) recovers the Jaccard distance with no dense N × N N\times N intermediate—with the full derivation in the released code. 5 Stress-Testing the Diversity Premise 5.1 Branch-level diagnostics Guided by Proposition 1, we measure disagreement where it counts—retrieval behavior: 1. Per-branch retrieval : each branch’s standalone mAP/R1 (how strong is each stream?); 2. Top- k k Jaccard : overlap of two branches’ top-10 retrieval sets (do they return the same gallery images?); 3. Occlusion-saliency agreement : Pearson correlation and top-20% IoU of occlusion-sensitivity heatmaps [ 26 ] (do they look at the same regions?); 4. Complementary-correctness : fraction of queries one branch ranks correctly and the other does not (is there unique signal to harvest?). These complement representation-level tools such as CKA [ 17 ] : two branches can be CKA-dissimilar yet retrieve identically; retrieval-level measures bound fusion headroom directly. 5.2 Same-backbone multi-head: collapse into redundancy At convergence the four heads are statistically indistinguishable (spread 0.17) and concatenation delivers no statistically distinguishable gain over the best single head: a paired per-query bootstrap of the difference gives Δ \Delta (concat − - BoT-cls) = − 0.05 mAP =\textbf{$-0.05$ mAP} , 95% CI [ − 0.19 , + 0.09 ] [-0.19,+0.09] , covering zero. The paired form is essential here—the corresponding unpaired single-model CI has half-width ± 0.66 \pm 0.66 , far too wide to adjudicate a 0.05 difference; pairing cancels the shared query-set variance and shrinks the interval nearly fivefold. The diversity trajectory (Table 4 ) explains why the heads are redundant. In-domain replication on VeRi-776. The collapse is not specific to VeRi-Wild. Training the same Option A in-domain on VeRi-776 (575 IDs, 84.07 mAP) reproduces it: concatenation (84.07) again fails to beat the best single head (84.69), Δ = − 0.62 \Delta=-0.62 . A leave-one-out recipe ablation confirms the collapse is robust to the recipe and attributes the accuracy to two dominant positive levers: the ConvNeXt convolutional heads—replacing them with ResNet-Bottleneck heads costs + 6.4 +6.4 mAP , making the pure-ConvNeXt head choice the single largest recipe contribution rather than an architectural nicety—and the staged LR decay ( + 4.63 +4.63 ); the loss is neutral ( + 0.15 +0.15 ). One One component does not carry over. Full-depth features are harmful on VeRi-776: truncating the trunk one stage earlier, which doubles the spatial resolution fed to the heads, reaches 87.32 against 82.32 for full depth in a matched ablation ( − 5.0 -5.0 ). On VeRi-Wild the same substitution is neutral rather than harmful ( 88.69 truncated vs. 88.19 full-depth; the two runs differ in batch size and schedule length, so we read them as comparable, not ordered). Semantic depth is therefore not the lever the recipe search first suggested—spatial resolution is at least as valuable on both benchmarks—and we retain the full-depth system as our reference only because every analysis below is anchored on it. On the best VeRi-776 configuration a marginal Δ ​ ( concat − best head ) = + 0.58 \Delta(\text{concat}-\text{best head})=+0.58 (paired 95% CI [ + 0.49 , + 0.68 ] [+0.49,+0.68] ) does emerge, but an order of magnitude below the multi-branch literature’s gains, and it reverses to − 0.62 -0.62 under full-depth. Across both datasets and every configuration, concatenation moves the best single head by under one point in either direction: redundancy, not the premised diversity. Four branches produce one representation, four times. 5.3 Cross-backbone fusion: maximum heterogeneity, zero net gain Genuine heterogeneity at the starting line. With both backbones frozen, ConvNeXt and ViT-L occlusion saliencies correlate at only 0.30 (200-pair bootstrap 95% CI [0.26, 0.34]; top-20% IoU 0.20 [0.18, 0.22])—the lowest we measure anywhere, versus 0.96 for same-backbone heads, with non-overlapping confidence intervals (Table 5 )—confirming that CNN/Transformer representational differences [ 16 ] survive DINOv3 distillation at initialization. Our dual-backbone model (ConvNeXt full-depth + ViT-L [ 27 ] , two mutual-fusion cross-attention modules, learned fusion head, ∼ 560 {\sim}560 M training-time params; ∼ 404 {\sim}404 M on the deployment path, Section 6 ) peaks at 85.30 (E7) then declines for ten straight epochs to 83.36. The reversal coincides exactly with the LR schedule reaching its 2.5e-4 plateau, and the training loss spikes synchronously (7.55/7.90/8.21): the mAP turn, the LR plateau and the loss spikes align on the epoch axis, pinning the collapse to optimization rather than architecture. Restarting from the peak with LR × 0.1 \times 0.1 immediately recovers to 86.32 —confirming the same. At this rescued state we observe the only genuine fusion gain in this study : fused 86.32 vs. best single branch (cnx_g) 81.38, + 4.94 +4.94 , with Jaccard 0.535. But the comparison base is contaminated: joint training degraded the ConvNeXt to 81.38, far below the 88.19 the same backbone reaches alone. The fusion gain is real only relative to a base that fusion training itself weakened—and the fused 86.2–86.3 never approaches 88.19. Asymmetric frozen-anchor: giving fusion every advantage. We therefore transplant the converged 88.19 ConvNeXt system (all 350 weight keys of the four-head Option A backbone) and freeze it as a semantic anchor, training only the ViT, the fusion modules, and the fusion head. Two quantities must be kept distinct: the transplanted anchor is the full 8192-d Option A embedding (88.19), whereas cnx_g is a diagnostic 1024-d global-average-pool probe of the frozen trunk (one of four fusion-head inputs) that on its own reaches only 86.5 (Table 6 )—an untrained pool, not a head. We therefore do not claim a by-construction floor of 88.19: system-level accuracy requires the fusion head to recombine cnx_g with the ViT-enhanced components. What the frozen anchor does guarantee is anti-collapse, verified directly: on the same 2.5e-4 base-LR plateau that coincided with the symmetric run’s ten-epoch slide, all asymmetric runs hold stable across ViT learning rates 2.5e-5–1.125e-4 (fused 88.22 → \rightarrow 87.93 for the × 0.1 \times 0.1 run, labeled Asymmetric v1 in Fig. 1 )—isolating the frozen anchor, not any particular ViT rate, as the stabilizer. Three recipes plus a PEFT control. To preempt the objection that the ViT branch was under-trained, we train it under three full-fine-tuning recipes (Table 6 , Fig. 1 ). Because full fine-tuning of self-supervised ViTs is a documented source of instability—parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA [ 28 ] ) mitigates the catastrophic forgetting it induces [ 29 ] , consistent with [ 10 ] —we additionally report a LoRA control below, so the ceiling is not attributed to full fine-tuning by omission. This also locates the literature’s gains: against its own single-backbone readout (86.47)—the comparison multi-branch work typically makes—the same fused embedding shows + 1.75 +1.75 ; against an independently tuned single backbone, + 0.03 +0.03 (n.s.). The gain is a property of the baseline, not of the fusion. The bottleneck is branch strength, not fusion design. The same verdict holds inside the trained fusion: every re-weighting of its four components that raises the ViT’s contribution performs at or below the learned fusion head (87.96 baseline; worst − 1.64 -1.64 ), and reciprocal-rank fusion never exceeds the anchor’s single path—the fusion head’s down-weighting of the ViT is already optimal. Loss curves agree: the ViT branch’s classification loss stays hardest to fit while the fused loss tracks the frozen anchor’s. Nor is the ViT weak per se —frozen, it is the strongest bare backbone we test (18.56 zero-shot vs. ConvNeXt 14.63, ResNet50 3.77)—yet every fine-tuned configuration lands far below ConvNeXt. We probe three points on the fine-tuning spectrum. (i) A standalone ViT-L fine-tuned entirely outside the fusion topology (no anchor, no cross-attention) plateaus at 67.0 mAP (last row of Table 6 )— below even the ∼ 73 {\sim}73 the same ViT reaches as a branch inside the fusion, ruling out that gradient routing through the fusion head starved it. (ii) The three full-fine-tuning recipes cap at ∼ 73 {\sim}73 . (iii) A LoRA -adapted ViT branch (blocks 20–23, taken from our dual-backbone model) reaches 75.19 — above the full-fine-tuning ceiling, confirming that the ∼ 73 {\sim}73 figure is partly a symptom of full-fine-tuning fragility for self-supervised backbones [ 29 ] rather than a hard representational wall. Yet even this best ViT configuration (75.19) sits ∼ 13 {\sim}13 mAP below the ConvNeXt single backbone (88.19): the cross-backbone gap survives the PEFT control. The robust finding is therefore not a precise ∼ 73 {\sim}73 ceiling but the 13–15-point ViT-versus-ConvNeXt gap ( ∼ 15 {\sim}15 under full fine-tuning, ∼ 13 {\sim}13 with the strongest LoRA configuration) that persists across adaptation regimes, at this data scale and 256-px resolution and for this pretraining lineage—the scope within which we make the claim. Would the strongest ViT have fused? Our trained fusions reach branch strength ∼ 73 {\sim}73 ; the LoRA branch reaches 75.19 but was trained outside the anchor. We close that gap without retraining, by bounding what any fusion of these two representations could yield. Proposition 1 first confirms the diversity is real: over top-10 retrievals the LoRA-ViT contributes 0.62 correct gallery images per query that the single-backbone system misses (a + 8.4 % +8.4\% hit-set headroom on 35.2% of queries; Jaccard 0.54, far more heterogeneous than same-backbone heads at 0.79–0.84). Yet none of it is recoverable: an oracle score-level fusion—mixing weights tuned directly on the test set, an upper bound no learned fusion module can exceed—selects weight zero for the LoRA-ViT. Every non-zero weight is a net loss ( − 0.06 -0.06 at α = 0.3 \alpha{=}0.3 , − 0.33 -0.33 at 0.5 0.5 , − 2.34 -2.34 at equal weight): fusion inherits the ViT’s entire ranking, and the errors it injects outweigh the matches it recovers. One cannot take only its correct half. Two observations rule out that a mid-level module would behave differently: the trained cross-attention fusion is bounded at + 0.11 +0.11 mAP (paired 95% CI, above), and fused mAP decreases monotonically as the ViT strengthens—peaking at 88.22 while the ViT is still at 42.3, settling to 87.7–88.05 once it reaches ∼ 73 {\sim}73 . A gain at 75.19 would require that trend to reverse. Cross-backbone retrieval diversity is real; it is simply not fusible —the premise fails not at the diversity step but at the aggregation step. 5.4 Shared-teacher control: heterogeneity is not understated Both backbones distill from the same DINOv3 teacher, so one might worry that the heterogeneity we measure understates what independent pretraining lineages would provide—and that fusion could pay off for a more heterogeneous pair. We test this directly with linear CKA [ 17 ] over 2,500 VeRi-Wild images, each backbone frozen and globally average-pooled, comparing our shared-teacher pair (DINOv3-ConvNeXt vs. DINOv3-ViT) against an independent-lineage control (ImageNet-supervised ConvNeXt-B vs. ViT-L). The cross-architecture similarity of our shared-teacher pair is 0.561 — lower (more heterogeneous) than the 0.638 of the independently pretrained ImageNet pair. Independent lineage does not provide more heterogeneity here; if anything, ImageNet supervision, by driving both architectures toward the same label-defined decision boundary, homogenizes them, whereas self-supervised distillation preserves architecture-driven differences—consistent with observations that the training signal, not just the architecture, shapes representational similarity [ 17 , 18 ] . Our fusion pair is thus the most heterogeneous cross-architecture pairing we can construct—more so than a genuinely independent one—and fusion still yields zero net gain. This strengthens rather than qualifies Section 5-5.3 : the diversity is genuine and near-maximal, and it still does not pay. (Linear CKA measures representational similarity, a proxy; whether a fully independent backbone pair could fuse past the 88.19 single-backbone ceiling remains a concrete falsifier we state in Section 7 , item (a).) 5.5 Measure only at convergence Undertrained snapshots systematically mislead.
